1189	8 Related Work
1190	DetTrace’s unique reproducible container abstraction
1191	takes inspiration from many previous systems. We cate-
1192	gorize this previous work into record-and-replay systems,
1193	and deterministic execution systems.
1194	Many record and replay (RnR) systems have been
1195	proposed both from academia [ 40–46] and industry [ 47–
1196	49]. These systems record a trace of one nondeterministic
1197	execution to enable subsequent replay of that execution,
1198	typically for debugging purposes. These systems have
1199	broadly similar interception requirements as DetTrace,
1200	since system calls are a prime source of irreproducibility
1201	that must be recorded in the trace. DetTrace borrows
1202	some implementation techniques from Mozilla’s rr [ 47]
1203	as it also relies on ptrace (a quantitative comparison
1204	with rr appears in Section 7.1.3). Many RnR systems
1205	target multithreaded workloads, as those are very chal-
1206	lenging to debug without RnR support, and provide
1207	high-performance parallel recording and replaying.
1208	Deterministic execution schemes enforce determin-
1209	ism during program execution. Deterministic operating
1210	systems tackle several of the systems issues we describe
1211	in this paper, providing deterministic versions of OS
1212	abstractions like processes and threads. While Determi-
1213	nator [12] provides new OS abstractions for deterministic
1214	fork-join parallelism, and DDOS [ 13] focuses on local
1215	network interactions, dOS [ 14] is closer to our work
1216	in offering a deterministic process group abstraction.
1217	The shim abstraction in dOS bears similarity to Linux’s
1218	ptrace API. Unlike DetTrace, dOS supports parallel exe-
1219	cution of both threads and processes. However, dOS uses
1220	RnR for filesystem interactions, defining the boundaries
1221	of its determinism abstraction too narrowly to be useful
1222	for software builds which interact extensively with the
1223	filesystem. More generally, a custom OS is a heavyweight
1224	prerequisite to perform deterministic computation, and
1225	existing deterministic OSes have not evaluated portabil-
1226	ity across different microarchitectures.
1227	Other deterministic execution schemes focus on a sin-
1228	gle multithreaded process, determinizing interactions
1229	through shared memory. Some schemes target arbitrary
1230	binary programs [50–58], providing generality at a mod-
1231	est performance overhead. Other schemes leverage lan-
1232	guage support to provide determinism for Haskell [ 10,
1233	26, 59–62] or Java [9, 63] programs. Whether language-
1234	agnostic or specific, these approaches eliminate the in-
1235	fluence of thread scheduling, but do not determinize IO
1236	interactions with the underlying OS and filesystem. The
1237	scope of their guarantees is thus too small to be useful
1238	for reproducible builds. One exception is DetFlow [ 11]
1239	which provides deterministic parallel execution for batch
1240	jobs, though it lacks robust system call interception and
1241	requires a coordinator layer written in Haskell.
1242	9 Conclusions
1243	We have described the design and implementation of Det-
1244	Trace, which provides a new reproducible container ab-
1245	straction. DetTrace automatically provides reproducibil-
1246	ity for software builds, bioinformatics processing and
1247	ML workflows without requiring any changes to the
1248	hardware, OS, or application code. To facilitate further
1249	experimentation with DetTrace, we plan to open-source
1250	its code upon publication.

1540	A.3 Description
1541	A.3.1 How delivered. The latest version of DetTrace can
1542	be found on GitHub. A more permanent but perhaps older
1543	version exists at
1544	https://zenodo.org/record/3562526.
1545	A.3.2 Hardware dependencies. The DetTrace proto-
1546	type currently only works for x86-64 Intel CPUs. While
1547	not strictly necessary, the CPU must have support for in-
1548	tercepting certain nondeterministic CPU instructions, e.g.
1549	CPUID.
1550	A.3.3 Software dependencies. DetTrace works well with
1551	kernel versions 4.8 and< 5.3 (only minor modifications should
1552	be necessary to allow DetTrace to work in newer kernel ver-
1553	sions). Kernel version ≤ 4.8 use a slower ptrace implementa-
1554	tion (more details in paper above), making overall execution
1555	of DetTrace slower. Kernel version ≥ 4.12 are required for
1556	OS support for CPUID interception. Currently DetTrace has
1557	a few dependencies:
1558	• libssl: Hashing implementation for bytes from read
1559	system call (Useful for debugging nondeterministic
1560	bytes read from pipe).
1561	• libseccomp: Helper library for finer-grained system call
1562	filtering using seccomp-bpf.
1563	• libarchive: Unpackaging archive files used by DetTrace.
1564	• libelfin: ELF/DWARF parser.
1565	• libfuse: Running tests only. Used for filesystem tests.
1566	These dependencies are fairly common and should be easy
1567	to install from your Linux distro’s package manager. For
1568	Apt these are libarchive-dev, libssl-dev, and libseccomp-dev,
1569	libelfin-dev, and libfuse-dev.
1570	DetTrace relies on various Linux namespaces for isolation
1571	and determinism. Some systems disable user namespaces
1572	by default. You may encounter a clone failed: operation not
1573	permitted error. If so, please enable user namespace access
1574	(the exact method may depend on your distro and OS ver-
1575	sion). Furthermore, Linux does not allow user namespaces
1576	for processes whose root is not / (the chroot system call was
1577	executed at some point).
1578	A.3.4 Data sets. While DetTrace is designed to enforce
1579	reproducibility for arbitrary computation, the prototype im-
1580	plementation was overfitted to work with Debian packages
1581	and chroot environments. The Debian Apt Package Reposi-
1582	tory and chroot images available through debootstrap may
1583	be of interest. Our prototype built mostly Debian Wheezy
1584	packages, newer Debian version may execute system calls not
1585	currently implemented in DetTrace.
1586	A.4 Installation
1587	DetTrace uses a standard Makefile for compilation. Assuming
1588	you have the all the software dependencies (above), and a
1589	C++ compiler supporting C++14, running make in the root
1590	directory of the repository will generate the DetTrace binary
1591	under bin/. DetTrace may also be statically linked using
1592	make static assuming all the correct dependencies are present
1593	as statically linkable objects. DetTrace may be installed
1594	anywhere on the system by moving the bin/ directory along
1595	with the root/ directory. This directory structure must be
1596	maintained as the DetTrace binary always expects root/ to
1597	be located ../root relative to the location of the DetTrace
1598	binary (see reasoning below).
1599	The word chroot is unfortunately overloaded, both referring
1600	to the Linux system call which changes the location of the
1601	root directory for a process, and for the concept of a directory
1602	tree which ”look like” a Linux filesystem, containing all the
1603	binaries, libraries, and special files (e.g. /proc, /dev) necessary
1604	for a Linux system to function.
1605	The Debian command debootstrap is an easy way to get
1606	such a chroot environment. For more information see:
1607	https://wiki.debian.org/chroot.
1608	If you’re using a different Linux distribution, you should
1609	consult the documentation to find the appropriate way to
1610	install a chroot. You can install debootstrap from the Apt
1611	repository. sudo apt install debootstrap .
1612	One can install a Stretch Debian chroot by running the
1613	commands:
1614	$ mkdir stretch
1615	$ sudo debootstrap stretch stretch/ \
1616	http://deb.debian.org/debian
1617	Unfortunately, this requires root to work. Once you have
1618	downloaded the chroot, you should have a ‘stretch‘ directory
1619	which we can ‘ls‘:
1620	$ ls stretch
1621	bin/ dev/ home/ lib64/ mnt/ proc/ run/
1622	boot/ etc/ lib/ media/ opt/ root/ sbin/
1623	As you can see, this looks just like a Linux filesystem tree.
1624	DetTrace accepts any such chroot to be used as the starting
1625	image. As DetTrace will be using the files in ‘stretch‘ we need
1626	to ensure the permissions are correct (more information can
1627	be found at https://wiki.debian.org/chroot):
1628	sudo chgrp -R $USER stretch/
1629	sudo chown -R $USER stretch/
1630	You are now ready to use DetTrace and the chroot (see
1631	below).
1632	
1633	PAGE 16
1634	ASPLOS ’20, March 16–20, 2020, Lausanne, Switzerland Navarro Leija et al.
1635	A.5 Experiment workflow
1636	DetTrace is a command line tool which makes it easy to make
1637	computation reproducible. You can simply prepend the com-
1638	mand you are interested in determinizing with./path/to/dettrace.
1639	For example:
1640	$ ./bin/dettrace ls -ahl
1641	-rw-r--r-- 1 root ... Jan 1 1970 initramfs.cpio
1642	drwxr-xr-x 1 root ... Jan 1 1970 root
1643	-rw-r--r-- 1 root ... Jan 1 1970 shell.nix
1644	drwxr-xr-x 1 root ... Jan 1 1970 src
1645	...
1646	Note the dates of all files are now deterministic! DetTrace
1647	will determinize the specified program along with any subpro-
1648	cesses that are spawned. Furthermore, DetTrace containerizes
1649	the program to guarantee a reproducible starting filesystem.
1650	Similarly we may create a file and then stat the file with
1651	DetTrace:
1652	$ touch foo.txt
1653	$ ./bin/dettrace stat foo.txt
1654	File: foo.txt
1655	Size: 0 Blocks: 1 IO Block: 512 ...
1656	Device: 1h/1d Inode: 8 Links: 1
1657	Access: (0644/-rw-r--r--) Uid: ...
1658	Access: 1970-01-01 00:00:00.000000000 +0000
1659	Modify: 1970-01-01 00:00:00.000000000 +0000
1660	Change: 1970-01-01 00:00:00.000000000 +0000
1661	Birth: -
1662	Notice a lot of the file’s metadata is now deterministic!
1663	We didn’t specify a container when calling DetTrace with
1664	these simple commands. Yet, when running commands:
1665	$ ./bin/dettrace pwd
1666	/build
1667	$./bin/dettrace ls /
1668	bin/ build/ dettrace/ dev/ etc/ lib/ ...
1669	We see the current working directory (CWD) is /build and
1670	listing the root directory looks vastly different from the
1671	host’s root directory. This is because when no container
1672	is specified DetTrace will create a minimal one based on
1673	the root/ directory found at the top level of the DetTrace
1674	repository.
1675	Running:
1676	$ ls root
1677	bin/ build/ dettrace/ dev/ etc/ lib/ ...
1678	We can see this directory holds what looks like a minimal
1679	Linux filesystem. For this reason, DetTrace needs to be able to
1680	find the root/ directory, which DetTrace expects will always
1681	be ../root/ relative to the location of the binary.
1682	While running the command without a chroot is easy, it
1683	does not guarantee reproducibility since the starting filesys-
1684	tem state may be different from run to run. Therefore we
1685	use the chroot flag to specify the chroot image created in the
1686	build step (see above). We can use this chroot as the starting
1687	image for DetTrace:
1688	./bin/dettrace --chroot path/to/stretch/ ls
1689	This command will now run deterministically using the
1690	chroot as the starting image. DetTrace also supports running
1691	inside Docker containers, see the Makefile and Dockerfile to
1692	see how this is done for our own tests.
1693	A chroot or containerized environment is standard and
1694	recommend way to use DetTrace.
1695	A.6 Evaluation and expected result
1696	Any program running under DetTrace is expected to produce
1697	the output of the program with a deterministic version of the
1698	output. So running the date command multiple times will
1699	produce the same result.
1700	$ ./bin/dettrace date
1701	Sun Aug 8 22:00:00 UTC 1993
1702	$ ./bin/dettrace date
1703	Sun Aug 8 22:00:00 UTC 1993
1704	DetTrace comes with dozens of sample nondeterministic
1705	programs meant to stress test different sources of nondeter-
1706	minism found in programs. These programs are designed to
1707	be nondeterministic, and have an expected, deterministic,
1708	output when running under DetTrace. You may test your
1709	installation by running make test to run all our sample pro-
1710	grams and integration tests. If docker is installed you may run
1711	make test-docker to run the same tests under a Docker envi-
1712	ronment instead. Docker is the preferred way to run the tests
1713	as it handles hard to reproduce sources of unreproducibility
1714	seen in the wild.
1715	Let’s do a reproducible build! For simplicity we will use
1716	DetTrace itself as the program to build reproducibly. From
1717	the root directory of the DetTrace repository:
1718	./bin/dettrace make -C src/
1719	This will build DetTrace deterministically under DetTrace.
1720	You can use a program like hashdeep to hash the binary
1721	outputs of programs and ensure the results are deterministic
1722	across executions.
1723	A.7 Experiment customization
1724	Dettrace has several command line options which may be
1725	useful:
1726	• –debug N : Verbose debug output for DetTrace. Prints
1727	extra information about system calls, instructions, and
1728	OS events that DetTrace is intercepting. Useful for
1729	debugging failures or determinism bugs.
1730	• –working-dir: By default DetTrace “bind mounts” the
1731	CWD inside the container, this makes working without
1732	chroots easy and seamless. However, when working
1733	with chroots we probably don’t want the arbitrary
1734	CWD to be moved inside the chroot. Instead we want
1735	to specify a directory inside the chroot. This flag allows
1736	you to specify a CWD inside the chroot.

natively in parallel, 2) natively but with TensorFlow con-
figured to use a single thread and 3) with DetTrace. Since
TensorFlow uses thread-level parallelism via OpenMP,
DetTrace’s serialized threading incurs a large slowdown
over native parallel execution on 16 cores: it is 17.49×
slower on alexnet and 11.94× on cifar10. Compared to se-
rialized native execution, however, DetTrace fares much
better with slowdowns of 1.51× and 1.08×, respectively,
reinforcing that DetTrace exacts a small performance
price for non-threaded compute-bound workloads.
8 Related Work
DetTrace’s unique reproducible container abstraction
takes inspiration from many previous systems. We cate-
gorize this previous work into record-and-replay systems,
and deterministic execution systems.
Many record and replay (RnR) systems have been
proposed both from academia [ 40–46] and industry [ 47–
49]. These systems record a trace of one nondeterministic
execution to enable subsequent replay of that execution,
typically for debugging purposes. These systems have
broadly similar interception requirements as DetTrace,
since system calls are a prime source of irreproducibility
that must be recorded in the trace. DetTrace borrows
some implementation techniques from Mozilla’s rr [ 47]
as it also relies on ptrace (a quantitative comparison
with rr appears in Section 7.1.3). Many RnR systems
target multithreaded workloads, as those are very chal-
lenging to debug without RnR support, and provide
high-performance parallel recording and replaying.
Deterministic execution schemes enforce determin-
ism during program execution. Deterministic operating
systems tackle several of the systems issues we describe
in this paper, providing deterministic versions of OS
abstractions like processes and threads. While Determi-
nator [12] provides new OS abstractions for deterministic
fork-join parallelism, and DDOS [ 13] focuses on local
network interactions, dOS [ 14] is closer to our work
in offering a deterministic process group abstraction.
The shim abstraction in dOS bears similarity to Linux’s
ptrace API. Unlike DetTrace, dOS supports parallel exe-
cution of both threads and processes. However, dOS uses
RnR for filesystem interactions, defining the boundaries
of its determinism abstraction too narrowly to be useful
for software builds which interact extensively with the
filesystem. More generally, a custom OS is a heavyweight
prerequisite to perform deterministic computation, and
existing deterministic OSes have not evaluated portabil-
ity across different microarchitectures.
Other deterministic execution schemes focus on a sin-
gle multithreaded process, determinizing interactions
through shared memory. Some schemes target arbitrary
binary programs [50–58], providing generality at a mod-
est performance overhead. Other schemes leverage lan-
guage support to provide determinism for Haskell [ 10,
26, 59–62] or Java [9, 63] programs. Whether language-
agnostic or specific, these approaches eliminate the in-
fluence of thread scheduling, but do not determinize IO
interactions with the underlying OS and filesystem. The
scope of their guarantees is thus too small to be useful
for reproducible builds. One exception is DetFlow [ 11]
which provides deterministic parallel execution for batch
jobs, though it lacks robust system call interception and
requires a coordinator layer written in Haskell.
9 Conclusions
We have described the design and implementation of Det-
Trace, which provides a new reproducible container ab-
straction. DetTrace automatically provides reproducibil-
ity for software builds, bioinformatics processing and
ML workflows without requiring any changes to the
hardware, OS, or application code. To facilitate further
experimentation with DetTrace, we plan to open-source
its code upon publication.

A Artifact Appendix
A.1 Abstract
This artifact description gives an overview of the com-
mand line interface for DetTrace as well as common
DetTrace workflows. We describe the steps necessary
to build DetTrace, software dependencies, hardware re-
quirements, and compiler toolchains. Furthermore, we
show various example use-cases for DetTrace and using
chroot environments.
A.2 Artifact check-list (meta-information)
• Program: DetTrace: A Deterministic Container.
• Compilation: Any C++ compiler with C++14 sup-
port. Verified to compile with both g++ and clang++.

PAGE 15
Reproducible Containers ASPLOS ’20, March 16–20, 2020, Lausanne, Switzerland
• Run-time environment: Linux x86-64. Optimized
for kernel versions ≥ 4.8. Works on ≤ 4.8 kernel version
using slower methods (see paper for more information).
Kernel version ≥ 4.12 required for CPUID intercep-
tion. DetTrace is untested for kernel version ≥ 5.13
but should work with minor modifications or future
updates. Linux namespaces enabled required.
• Hardware: Intel x86-64 CPU. To intercept CPUID,
the CPU must support this feature.
• Output: DetTrace will produce a deterministic, re-
producible output of whichever command runs under
it. (See more below).
• Publicly available?: Yes
• Code licenses (if publicly available)?: MIT
• Archived (provide DOI)?: 10.5281/zenodo.3562526
A.3 Description
A.3.1 How delivered. The latest version of DetTrace can
be found on GitHub. A more permanent but perhaps older
version exists at
https://zenodo.org/record/3562526.
A.3.2 Hardware dependencies. The DetTrace proto-
type currently only works for x86-64 Intel CPUs. While
not strictly necessary, the CPU must have support for in-
tercepting certain nondeterministic CPU instructions, e.g.
CPUID.
A.3.3 Software dependencies. DetTrace works well with
kernel versions 4.8 and< 5.3 (only minor modifications should
be necessary to allow DetTrace to work in newer kernel ver-
sions). Kernel version ≤ 4.8 use a slower ptrace implementa-
tion (more details in paper above), making overall execution
of DetTrace slower. Kernel version ≥ 4.12 are required for
OS support for CPUID interception. Currently DetTrace has
a few dependencies:
• libssl: Hashing implementation for bytes from read
system call (Useful for debugging nondeterministic
bytes read from pipe).
• libseccomp: Helper library for finer-grained system call
filtering using seccomp-bpf.
• libarchive: Unpackaging archive files used by DetTrace.
• libelfin: ELF/DWARF parser.
• libfuse: Running tests only. Used for filesystem tests.
These dependencies are fairly common and should be easy
to install from your Linux distro’s package manager. For
Apt these are libarchive-dev, libssl-dev, and libseccomp-dev,
libelfin-dev, and libfuse-dev.
DetTrace relies on various Linux namespaces for isolation
and determinism. Some systems disable user namespaces
by default. You may encounter a clone failed: operation not
permitted error. If so, please enable user namespace access
(the exact method may depend on your distro and OS ver-
sion). Furthermore, Linux does not allow user namespaces
for processes whose root is not / (the chroot system call was
executed at some point).
A.3.4 Data sets. While DetTrace is designed to enforce
reproducibility for arbitrary computation, the prototype im-
plementation was overfitted to work with Debian packages
and chroot environments. The Debian Apt Package Reposi-
tory and chroot images available through debootstrap may
be of interest. Our prototype built mostly Debian Wheezy
packages, newer Debian version may execute system calls not
currently implemented in DetTrace.
A.4 Installation
DetTrace uses a standard Makefile for compilation. Assuming
you have the all the software dependencies (above), and a
C++ compiler supporting C++14, running make in the root
directory of the repository will generate the DetTrace binary
under bin/. DetTrace may also be statically linked using
make static assuming all the correct dependencies are present
as statically linkable objects. DetTrace may be installed
anywhere on the system by moving the bin/ directory along
with the root/ directory. This directory structure must be
maintained as the DetTrace binary always expects root/ to
be located ../root relative to the location of the DetTrace
binary (see reasoning below).
The word chroot is unfortunately overloaded, both referring
to the Linux system call which changes the location of the
root directory for a process, and for the concept of a directory
tree which ”look like” a Linux filesystem, containing all the
binaries, libraries, and special files (e.g. /proc, /dev) necessary
for a Linux system to function.
The Debian command debootstrap is an easy way to get
such a chroot environment. For more information see:
https://wiki.debian.org/chroot.
If you’re using a different Linux distribution, you should
consult the documentation to find the appropriate way to
install a chroot. You can install debootstrap from the Apt
repository. sudo apt install debootstrap .
One can install a Stretch Debian chroot by running the
commands:
$ mkdir stretch
$ sudo debootstrap stretch stretch/ \
http://deb.debian.org/debian
Unfortunately, this requires root to work. Once you have
downloaded the chroot, you should have a ‘stretch‘ directory
which we can ‘ls‘:
$ ls stretch
bin/ dev/ home/ lib64/ mnt/ proc/ run/
boot/ etc/ lib/ media/ opt/ root/ sbin/
As you can see, this looks just like a Linux filesystem tree.
DetTrace accepts any such chroot to be used as the starting
image. As DetTrace will be using the files in ‘stretch‘ we need
to ensure the permissions are correct (more information can
be found at https://wiki.debian.org/chroot):
sudo chgrp -R $USER stretch/
sudo chown -R $USER stretch/
You are now ready to use DetTrace and the chroot (see
below).

PAGE 16
ASPLOS ’20, March 16–20, 2020, Lausanne, Switzerland Navarro Leija et al.
A.5 Experiment workflow
DetTrace is a command line tool which makes it easy to make
computation reproducible. You can simply prepend the com-
mand you are interested in determinizing with./path/to/dettrace.
For example:
$ ./bin/dettrace ls -ahl
-rw-r--r-- 1 root ... Jan 1 1970 initramfs.cpio
drwxr-xr-x 1 root ... Jan 1 1970 root
-rw-r--r-- 1 root ... Jan 1 1970 shell.nix
drwxr-xr-x 1 root ... Jan 1 1970 src
...
Note the dates of all files are now deterministic! DetTrace
will determinize the specified program along with any subpro-
cesses that are spawned. Furthermore, DetTrace containerizes
the program to guarantee a reproducible starting filesystem.
Similarly we may create a file and then stat the file with
DetTrace:
$ touch foo.txt
$ ./bin/dettrace stat foo.txt
File: foo.txt
Size: 0 Blocks: 1 IO Block: 512 ...
Device: 1h/1d Inode: 8 Links: 1
Access: (0644/-rw-r--r--) Uid: ...
Access: 1970-01-01 00:00:00.000000000 +0000
Modify: 1970-01-01 00:00:00.000000000 +0000
Change: 1970-01-01 00:00:00.000000000 +0000
Birth: -
Notice a lot of the file’s metadata is now deterministic!
We didn’t specify a container when calling DetTrace with
these simple commands. Yet, when running commands:
$ ./bin/dettrace pwd
/build
$./bin/dettrace ls /
bin/ build/ dettrace/ dev/ etc/ lib/ ...
We see the current working directory (CWD) is /build and
listing the root directory looks vastly different from the
host’s root directory. This is because when no container
is specified DetTrace will create a minimal one based on
the root/ directory found at the top level of the DetTrace
repository.
Running:
$ ls root
bin/ build/ dettrace/ dev/ etc/ lib/ ...
We can see this directory holds what looks like a minimal
Linux filesystem. For this reason, DetTrace needs to be able to
find the root/ directory, which DetTrace expects will always
be ../root/ relative to the location of the binary.
While running the command without a chroot is easy, it
does not guarantee reproducibility since the starting filesys-
tem state may be different from run to run. Therefore we
use the chroot flag to specify the chroot image created in the
build step (see above). We can use this chroot as the starting
image for DetTrace:
./bin/dettrace --chroot path/to/stretch/ ls
This command will now run deterministically using the
chroot as the starting image. DetTrace also supports running
inside Docker containers, see the Makefile and Dockerfile to
see how this is done for our own tests.
A chroot or containerized environment is standard and
recommend way to use DetTrace.
A.6 Evaluation and expected result
Any program running under DetTrace is expected to produce
the output of the program with a deterministic version of the
output. So running the date command multiple times will
produce the same result.
$ ./bin/dettrace date
Sun Aug 8 22:00:00 UTC 1993
$ ./bin/dettrace date
Sun Aug 8 22:00:00 UTC 1993
DetTrace comes with dozens of sample nondeterministic
programs meant to stress test different sources of nondeter-
minism found in programs. These programs are designed to
be nondeterministic, and have an expected, deterministic,
output when running under DetTrace. You may test your
installation by running make test to run all our sample pro-
grams and integration tests. If docker is installed you may run
make test-docker to run the same tests under a Docker envi-
ronment instead. Docker is the preferred way to run the tests
as it handles hard to reproduce sources of unreproducibility
seen in the wild.
Let’s do a reproducible build! For simplicity we will use
DetTrace itself as the program to build reproducibly. From
the root directory of the DetTrace repository:
./bin/dettrace make -C src/
This will build DetTrace deterministically under DetTrace.
You can use a program like hashdeep to hash the binary
outputs of programs and ensure the results are deterministic
across executions.
A.7 Experiment customization
Dettrace has several command line options which may be
useful:
• –debug N : Verbose debug output for DetTrace. Prints
extra information about system calls, instructions, and
OS events that DetTrace is intercepting. Useful for
debugging failures or determinism bugs.
• –working-dir: By default DetTrace “bind mounts” the
CWD inside the container, this makes working without
chroots easy and seamless. However, when working
with chroots we probably don’t want the arbitrary
CWD to be moved inside the chroot. Instead we want
to specify a directory inside the chroot. This flag allows
you to specify a CWD inside the chroot.

1	# PROJECT VISION — Coordinator Prime Directive
2	
3	**Purpose:** This is the standing directive for the dev-hermit coordinator. Re-read every 1-2 hours. It prevents drift, lost inertia, and distraction.
4	
5	## Mission
6	
7	Aggressively drive hermit toward its final form: a production-grade deterministic execution engine with multiple backends (ptrace, KVM, Liteinst first party, plus DBT, e9patch, sabre with 3rd party deps) that all produce identical behavior/logs/memory, i.e. PARITY, plus record/replay and chaos concurrency testing that is equally broadly-compatible with arbitrary guest programs.
8	
9	Don't forget your general princples around CLEAR and SPECIFIC communication (which programs ran what under what mode and which branch/version was experimented with?) and presenting EVIDENCE for claims, including wherever possible reproducer commands.
10	
11	## Applications
12	
13	All the internal implementation priorities below are focused on making hermit USEFUL on real applications, which currently include but are not limited to:
14	
15	 - Linux kernel (and driver, and file system) concurrency testing and debugging inside QEMU inside hermit. Example milestones include getting our Linux demos running on non-ptrace hermit backends with improved performance.
16	 - Reproducible builds: including unblocking a watertight content addressable store mode for Nix, and being adoption ready for the Debian Reproducible Builds project or other distros or package managers.  Example milestones include enabling parallelism in detcore so `make -j` can use real parallelism, ideally with minimal determinism overhead from an efficient (non-ptrace) Reverie backend.
17	 - Record/replay debugging of userspace apps a la Mozilla rr. Example milestones include recording firefox (controlled by playwright) like rr originally targetted.
18	
19	## Priorities
20	
21	We expand compatibility across a set of tracked programs, most of which are part of the CI suite (but we can do periodic testing outside of it). We have have a common denominator for ALL tests in our CI manifests, and terminology for "cells" (mode x backend x test) which should monotonically increase in total coverage, both for DETERMINISM and for the stronger PARITY level of achievement (i.e. backend X runs program Y deterministically AND bitwise identical to the ptrace reference impl).
22	
23	Hermit has a series of modes:
24	
25	0. **Smoke test** -- running through hermit at all, with enforcement less than --strict, is a good first step on a new application but is not something we use as a goal (though "minimal dosing" of hermit is useful for reproducible builds).
26	1. **Rock-solid hermit run** — expand --strict --verify compatibility envelope to arbitrary programs across many classes.
27	2. **Record/replay** — expand R/R to match --verify coverage (e.g. fix pipe deadlocks), perodically compare against mature "rr"
28	3. Chaos mode and hermit analyze for concurency testing and race localization.
29	
30	Then the above modes can run in each of the backends, with running in non-ptrace backends being the expanding frontier that we need to drive.
31	
32	## Mode Expansion Mandate
33	
34	Every mode must catch up to the one before it, and advanced, higher-perf backends must catch up with the reference one:
35	- Example: 300 programs in --strict --verify → same 300 in record/replay → same in DBT → same in KVM, and the denominator are always the e2e tests we planned in the overhaul.
36	- There is NO stopping while trailing modes are weaker
37	- Always add NEW programs to coverage even as trailing modes catch up
38	
39	Agents will constantly try to put up fake results that mislead you, where they have mocked up something partial that is NOT the real thing we want. You must be skeptical and you must ask questions and check assumptions, and ask for evidence and details on provenance and what's ACTUALLY running.
40	
41	## Operations and Regulation
42	
43	1. **Land PRs, keep main green, zero compile warnings**
44	2. **Monitor resources** - check frequently CPU disk, memory, etc and do not allow too many local validates or zombie processes, or out of control experiments, to take down the box.
45	3. **Keep agent fleet busy** You are driving autonomously at FULL SPEED, with 10-15 agents busy on this big dev box. You have multiple lines of P0 work and massive open-ended backlogs. Pre-generate parallel work in the task graph.
46	4. **Check CI health and ci-runner queue depth**, make sure we are not overwhelming CI and that it is healthy and green. Get as close to zero open PRs as you can, and not PRs than agents. Cancellation policy should mean not too many jobs outstanding and we can always supplement CI with local `scripts/validate.rs` / locally-validated receipt protocol. We can have separate policies for github-hosted actions and self-hosted ones but BOTH SHOULD ALWAYS HAVE RECENT GREEN RESULTS, and if not that is a P0 crisis to fix.
47	5. **Clean repo state** — minimal open PRs, branches deleted after merge, `git status` clean in both parent and hermit/reverie checkouts
48	
49	## Failure Modes to Avoid
50	
51	1. **Lost inertia:** "0 busy, 0 ready" is a P0 alarm, not "nothing to do." Generate work immediately.
52	2. **Heartbeat/fleet-monitor paused:** NEVER pause these workflows. They are mission-critical safety nets.
53	3. **Agent exhaustion:** Try to /compact agents before they run out of context, but when agents hit 100% context, spawn fresh ones immediately at `~/work/dev-hermit/hermit`. Don't let all agents exhaust simultaneously.
54	4. **Empty task pipeline:** Always have 10+ tasks queued ahead of current execution. Pre-generate work.
55	5. **Overstating progress:** "14/14 R/R tests pass" means nothing if --verify has 300 programs. Measure gaps, not victories.
56	6. **Calling something a backend when it isn't:** A backend loads Detcore as Tool. One shared copy of the code. Prototypes and stubs are NOT backends.
57	7. **Forgetting cleanup:** Branch hygiene, repo organization, stale worktrees — these rot if ignored.
58	8. **Waiting for user review:** Do own review iterations. Don't block on human review. Use adversarial agent review.
59	9. **Single-threaded thinking:** Debugging is parallelizable. Burst agents for root-causing. Implementation can parallelize across subsystems.
60	10. **Stale context reuse:** Restart agents when their context is stale or full. Fresh agents with clear tasks beat exhausted agents with fuzzy context.
61	11. **Broken CI, agents ignoring it:** CI is red but agents locally validate to land, not fixing the problem.
62	
63	## Autonomous Operation Protocol
64	
65	- **Generate work continuously.** Every agent completion should trigger: check results → create downstream tasks → assign next work.
66	- **Own PR iterations.** Adversarial review by different agent, fix issues, land. Don't wait.
67	- **Report precisely, with provenance.** State WHERE (main, feature branch, PR #N). Qualify results (L0/L1/L2). Never unqualified "passing."
68	- **Keep 10+ agents busy** at all times. If fewer are busy, spawn or generate work.
69	- **Path validation before spawn.** Check cwd exists before spawning agents.
70	- **Commit immediately, push immediately.** No work left uncommitted or unpushed.
71	
72	## Architecture North Stars
73	
74	### Hermit run
75	
76	Runs essentially arbitrary user space Linux programs under --strict --verify with perfect deterministic execution. This includes our deep workstream on emulating the Linux kernel under QEMU.
77	
78	Allows advanced chaos mode which perturbs program schedule orders and is compatible with all programs that normal --strict --verify runs on.
79	
80	### Hermit record / replay
81	
82	Works for everything rr does. Eventually is configurable from an rr-like mode to a `hermit run` mode that ONLY records external communication at the container boundary (and optionally file system boundary).
83	
84	### Drive Reverie BACKENDS
85	
86	Keep one fixed-purpose agent for each backend: "hermit-kvm", "hermit-dbi", "hermit-sabre", "hermit-liteinst", "hermit-e9patch".  Each will drive forward to have a complete and correct Reverie backend (working for arbitrary Reverie tools) plus hermit/detcore integration eventually supporting ALL the same guest programs deterministically as hermit/ptrace.
87	
88	### KVM Backend
89	Highest priority, will probably be our flagship backend.
90	```
91	hermit-cli → Detcore<KvmGuest> → KVM (gvisor model)
92	  Similar to gvisor (Go program as kernel, trap all syscalls in userspace) but with Detcore tool as the "operating system".
93	  NO hacks or temporary proof-of-concepts. Fully runs all hermit --strict --verify that ptrace can.
94	```
95	### LiteInst Backend
96	
97	Aside from KVM and ptrace, ALL other binary patching/instrumentation backends keep the Reverie local tool INSIDE the guest address space (communicating to the global state through RPC that shares code between reverie-liteinst, reverie-dbt, reverie-sabre, reverie-e9patch).
98	
99	Based on my instruction punning invention and our new reimplemntation (liteinst2), which provides DYNAMIC hooking of arbitrary instructions.
100	In this backend, we trap nondeterministic instructions (syscalls/cpuid/rdtsc/rdrand/etc) but on the first trap we patch them to hook directly into the guest.
101	
102	Our plan is to use LD_PRELOAD to infect the guest (and its children) and remove the need for ptrace as much as possible, but resort to a ptrace supervisor as a backup if there is a corner case we cannot handle.
103	
104	### DBT Backend
105	Dynamic Binary Translation based on DynamoRIO. This should be foolproof at catching nondeterministic instructions, and has the benefit that it can build branch-counting directly in, avoiding the problem of massive skid on PMU retired branch conditional timers. But it will probably fail on self-modifying code, e.g JVM JITs or QEMU TCG.
106	
107	```
108	hermit-cli → Detcore<DbtGuest> → DynamoRIO
109	  NO hacks or temporary proof-of-concepts. Fully runs all hermit --strict --verify that ptrace can.
110	```
111	
112	### Sabre Backend
113	Another binary patching backend, but at startup time it scans all application code.  With this one we use ptrace + sabre and hew closer to the design of the ptrace backend but try to optimize how many nondet instructions avoid traps.  However, ptrace needs to be able to redirect trapped instructions to in-guest handlers because the Reverie tool state lives in guest address spaces.
114	
115	### e9patch Backend
116	Based on instruction punning like LiteInst but at startup time.  We pair this with our own scanning for nondet instructions (CFG reconstruction), very similar to Sabre. But we try to share the same LD_PRELOAD injection method making this a close counterpart to the LiteInst backend.
117	
118	### Done = Identical (Parity)
119	A backend is done when ALL programs produce bitwise-identical output across all hermit reverie backends (ptrace/KVM/Liteinst/etc). Same memory hashes, same guest output, same exit codes.

- Example: 300 programs in --strict --verify → same 300 in record/replay → same in DBT → same in KVM, and the denominator are always the e2e tests we planned in the overhaul.

3. **Agent exhaustion:** Try to /compact agents before they run out of context, but when agents hit 100% context, spawn fresh ones immediately at `~/work/dev-hermit/hermit`. Don't let all agents exhaust simultaneously.
4. **Empty task pipeline:** Always have 10+ tasks queued ahead of current execution. Pre-generate work.

6. **Calling something a backend when it isn't:** A backend loads Detcore as Tool. One shared copy of the code. Prototypes and stubs are NOT backends.
7. **Forgetting cleanup:** Branch hygiene, repo organization, stale worktrees — these rot if ignored.
8. **Waiting for user review:** Do own review iterations. Don't block on human review. Use adversarial agent review.
9. **Single-threaded thinking:** Debugging is parallelizable. Burst agents for root-causing. Implementation can parallelize across subsystems.
10. **Stale context reuse:** Restart agents when their context is stale or full. Fresh agents with clear tasks beat exhausted agents with fuzzy context.

## Autonomous Operation Protocol

- **Generate work continuously.** Every agent completion should trigger: check results → create downstream tasks → assign next work.
- **Own PR iterations.** Adversarial review by different agent, fix issues, land. Don't wait.
- **Report precisely, with provenance.** State WHERE (main, feature branch, PR #N). Qualify results (L0/L1/L2). Never unqualified "passing."
- **Keep 10+ agents busy** at all times. If fewer are busy, spawn or generate work.
- **Path validation before spawn.** Check cwd exists before spawning agents.

## Architecture North Stars

### Hermit run

Runs essentially arbitrary user space Linux programs under --strict --verify with perfect deterministic execution. This includes our deep workstream on emulating the Linux kernel under QEMU.

### Drive Reverie BACKENDS

Keep one fixed-purpose agent for each backend: "hermit-kvm", "hermit-dbi", "hermit-sabre", "hermit-liteinst", "hermit-e9patch".  Each will drive forward to have a complete and correct Reverie backend (working for arbitrary Reverie tools) plus hermit/detcore integration eventually supporting ALL the same guest programs deterministically as hermit/ptrace.

### KVM Backend
Highest priority, will probably be our flagship backend.
```
hermit-cli → Detcore<KvmGuest> → KVM (gvisor model)
  Similar to gvisor (Go program as kernel, trap all syscalls in userspace) but with Detcore tool as the "operating system".
  NO hacks or temporary proof-of-concepts. Fully runs all hermit --strict --verify that ptrace can.
```
### LiteInst Backend

Aside from KVM and ptrace, ALL other binary patching/instrumentation backends keep the Reverie local tool INSIDE the guest address space (communicating to the global state through RPC that shares code between reverie-liteinst, reverie-dbt, reverie-sabre, reverie-e9patch).

Based on my instruction punning invention and our new reimplemntation (liteinst2), which provides DYNAMIC hooking of arbitrary instructions.
In this backend, we trap nondeterministic instructions (syscalls/cpuid/rdtsc/rdrand/etc) but on the first trap we patch them to hook directly into the guest.

Our plan is to use LD_PRELOAD to infect the guest (and its children) and remove the need for ptrace as much as possible, but resort to a ptrace supervisor as a backup if there is a corner case we cannot handle.

### DBT Backend
Dynamic Binary Translation based on DynamoRIO. This should be foolproof at catching nondeterministic instructions, and has the benefit that it can build branch-counting directly in, avoiding the problem of massive skid on PMU retired branch conditional timers. But it will probably fail on self-modifying code, e.g JVM JITs or QEMU TCG.

```
hermit-cli → Detcore<DbtGuest> → DynamoRIO
  NO hacks or temporary proof-of-concepts. Fully runs all hermit --strict --verify that ptrace can.
```

### Sabre Backend
Another binary patching backend, but at startup time it scans all application code.  With this one we use ptrace + sabre and hew closer to the design of the ptrace backend but try to optimize how many nondet instructions avoid traps.  However, ptrace needs to be able to redirect trapped instructions to in-guest handlers because the Reverie tool state lives in guest address spaces.

### e9patch Backend
Based on instruction punning like LiteInst but at startup time.  We pair this with our own scanning for nondet instructions (CFG reconstruction), very similar to Sabre. But we try to share the same LD_PRELOAD injection method making this a close counterpart to the LiteInst backend.

### Done = Identical (Parity)
A backend is done when ALL programs produce bitwise-identical output across all hermit reverie backends (ptrace/KVM/Liteinst/etc). Same memory hashes, same guest output, same exit codes.

5	This document consolidates the Hermit and Reverie research recorded in the

8	plan.

10	## Executive summary
11	
12	Hermit v2 should become a robust deterministic execution engine for real Linux
13	binaries, with reproducible run/record/replay, schedule stress and search, and
14	a lower-overhead execution backend. The longer-term Linux-kernel milestone is
15	to run a pinned QEMU/TCG VM under Hermit, combine it with an in-guest race
16	oracle, and make the host-side QEMU schedule a replayable input.
17	
18	The project has a functioning base, but several historical status claims need
19	qualification:
20	
21	- The current fork builds and its primary local validation passes. A current
22	  inventory on `main` counted 175 named Cargo cases: 173 pass and two doctests
23	  are ignored. The often-repeated "300+ ported tests" describes work attempted
24	  across branches and worktrees, not the authoritative coverage on `main`.
25	- Hosted CI is healthy. The self-hosted runner executes CPUID and PMU checks,
26	  but full Hermit integration coverage is not green: nested network namespace
27	  setup needs a `sysfs` mount that fails in the current runner container.
28	  Running the runner privileged or outside its container is the proven fix.
29	- Event-level schedule search works end to end. It localized both
30	  `hello_race` and `racewrite_nostdlib` to source lines with stack traces.
31	  Replay jitter, event alignment, disabled sub-event refinement, and weak
32	  endpoint validation prevent calling it a supported general feature yet.
33	- The restored SaBRe stack is a real runnable prototype, not just source
34	  archaeology. Its narrow raw-syscall path was about 13x faster than ptrace,
35	  but its in-process signal, thread, lifecycle, and API semantics remain the
36	  dominant risk. A useful synchronous backend is estimated at 5-8 weeks;
37	  broad parity is 12-20+ weeks with architectural caveats.
38	- DynamoRIO is the strongest maintained binary-instrumentation alternative.
39	  It deserves a time-boxed proof of concept before SaBRe becomes a strategic
40	  dependency.
41	- A `reverie-kvm` protocol skeleton exists and passes five unit tests, but it
42	  intentionally returns `SentryBridgeNotImplemented`. A production KVM path
43	  means integrating with a Linux ABI provider such as gVisor's Sentry, not
44	  merely issuing KVM ioctls. The estimate is 4-6 engineer-months for an MVP and
45	  9-15 engineer-months for broad parity and hardening.
46	- QEMU/TCG can boot under a deliberately relaxed Hermit configuration. Full
47	  deterministic mode is currently too slow and semantically incomplete. The
48	  measured boot uses 147,679 syscalls across 54 names; `ppoll`, futex timeout
49	  correctness, vectored I/O, inherited-file handling, and external helper
50	  state are the main path to a strict deterministic boot.
51	
52	The recommended order is: restore trustworthy green gates, fix real-binary
53	correctness and precise-PMU overhead, harden schedule search, then advance two
54	parallel bets - a measured fast-backend prototype and deterministic QEMU/TCG.
55	Do not begin the long KVM/Sentry program or open-ended kernel fuzzing until
56	those gates provide stable evidence.
57	
58	## Vision and success criteria
59	
60	Hermit v2 is a deterministic execution platform for arbitrary Linux ELF
61	binaries and their process trees. Its product capabilities are:
62	
63	1. Run arbitrary dynamically linked, multithreaded, signal-heavy programs with
64	   explicit boundaries for filesystem, network, and external inputs.
65	2. Record and replay executions faithfully, with actionable divergence
66	   diagnostics rather than hangs or opaque panics.
67	3. Explore scheduling interleavings in chaos mode and reproduce a selected
68	   outcome by seed and artifacts.
69	4. Search between passing and failing schedules, reduce the difference to a
70	   validated event ordering, and report stack/source context.
71	5. Provide at least one production-quality backend that avoids ptrace's
72	   syscall-stop cost while retaining a documented Reverie capability subset.
73	6. Allow non-communicating processes to run in parallel without abandoning the
74	   deterministic model.
75	7. Maintain comprehensive, resource-bounded CI for ordinary, PMU-dependent,
76	   namespace-dependent, record/replay, and schedule-search behavior.
77	
78	The QEMU/Linux milestone is a downstream application of those capabilities:
79	a pinned, immutable Linux VM under QEMU/TCG whose workload, oracle output, and
80	Hermit schedule can be replayed and reduced. Hermit supplies schedule control,
81	not the kernel race oracle; KCSAN, KASAN, LOCKDEP, panic/hang detection, or a
82	workload invariant must supply the failure predicate.

149	## Backend strategy
150	
151	### Ptrace baseline and performance
152	
153	Optimized default-mode measurements on an AMD EPYC host show why backend and
154	timer work must be treated separately:
155	
156	| Workload | Native | `hermit run` | Run overhead | `hermit record` | Record overhead |
157	| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
158	| `/bin/true`, 32 syscalls | 0.000784 s | 0.009830 s | 12.54x | 0.021831 s | 27.85x |
159	| CPU-only, 100M iterations | 0.236879 s | 9.409876 s | 39.72x | 9.541134 s | 40.28x |
160	| 30,032 syscalls | 0.083166 s | 1.751327 s | 21.06x | 1.349976 s | 16.23x |
161	| 256 thread create/join | 0.008435 s | 1.209288 s | 143.37x | 0.940607 s | 111.51x |
162	
163	Minimal ptrace with precise preemption disabled was still 10.98x on the
164	syscall workload and 9.76x on the thread workload, about 27.6 microseconds per
165	censused syscall and 0.289 ms per created thread. Those numbers are the target
166	for a faster syscall backend.
167	
168	The 40x CPU-only result is not syscall interception. Precise retired
169	conditional branch (RCB) preemption produced about 1.9 million context
170	switches; disabling preemption or using imprecise timers reduced the workload
171	to about 1.03x native. The AMD family 0x19 skid margin is 10,000, compared with
172	100 on Intel in the current model, creating a long single-step tail. Fast
173	syscall interception will not fix this. Timer calibration/algorithm work is an
174	independent P0 performance stream.

176	### SaBRe
177	
178	What works now:
179	
180	- The historical nine-package stack was restored.
181	- Upstream SaBRe `05816ee` builds; 69 tests pass unmodified, three are
182	  unsupported, and three portability failures pass with scratch-only fixes.
183	- Vendored plugin API sources restore linking; `reverie-sabre` passes 17/17
184	  unit tests.
185	- `riptrace` loads its plugin and traces `/bin/true`, `/bin/echo`, exec,
186	  fork/wait, exit-status propagation, and summary counting.
187	- A narrow, single-threaded 200,000-`getpid` probe took about 0.32-0.33 s under
188	  SaBRe versus 4.13-4.45 s under ptrace, roughly 13x faster. This is directional
189	  evidence, not a general workload claim.
190	
191	What blocks production use:
192	
193	- SaBRe has a separate synchronous in-process `Tool` API, not the shared async
194	  Reverie `Tool`/`Guest` contract.
195	- Signal handlers, TLS/guard state, bounded queues, `rt_sigaction`, and signal
196	  replacement/suppression are incomplete. A Python-class workload exposed
197	  guard and signal-queue failures during parity research.
198	- Fork/clone/vfork/clone3/exec lifecycle continuity, parent-aware state, abrupt
199	  exits, protected FDs, registers, stack allocation, backtraces, PMU timers,
200	  CPUID, and RDTSCP are incomplete or absent.
201	- Static rewriting does not cover every static, JIT, self-modifying, or
202	  dynamically generated syscall path. In-process instrumentation shares the
203	  guest's failure domain.
204	- Upstream is dormant: last push in 2022, no releases, no active successor,
205	  concentrated historical ownership, and GPL-3.0-or-later constraints.
206	
207	The runtime-stabilization branch has fixed the exit-timeout direction, an exit
208	race, queue saturation behavior, guarded signal callbacks, and part of SIGCHLD
209	handling. It is paused for the Reverie fork migration; `rt_sigaction`
210	virtualization, conformance gates, documentation, and verification remain.
211	
212	Recommended SaBRe boundary:
213	
214	- First deliver an explicit synchronous, syscall-centric backend extension.
215	- Do not change shared Reverie core abstractions merely to claim parity.
216	- Require common ptrace/SaBRe conformance workloads before promoting a
217	  capability.
218	- Budget 5-8 weeks for a credible x86-64 synchronous backend after the initial
219	  gate, and 12-20+ weeks for broad behavioral parity. Exact async callbacks,
220	  signal control, abrupt exits, unrewritten code, and aarch64 remain separate
221	  risks.
222	
223	### DynamoRIO and other instrumentation choices
224	
225	DynamoRIO is the strongest maintained alternative. Its active BSD core has
226	direct pre/post syscall callbacks, filtering, argument/number/result mutation,
227	suppression, and repeated injection. It handles translated/generated code and
228	has an active Rust wrapper. Its main risks are whole-process DBI overhead,
229	synchronous/no-std callbacks, and bridging safely to async tool logic.
230	
231	Run a time-boxed DynamoRIO proof of concept before selecting SaBRe as the
232	default fast backend. The acceptance suite must cover modify/suppress/inject,
233	clone/fork/vfork/exec, signals/EINTR, static and dynamic programs, JIT syscall
234	instructions, guest memory, and synchronous-to-async reentrancy. Benchmark an
235	empty client, a no-subscription client, and subscribed callbacks against
236	native, ptrace, and the SaBRe raw-syscall probe.
237	
238	Other findings:
239	
240	- Linux Syscall User Dispatch is the strongest purpose-built non-DBI primitive
241	  for a custom backend, especially as a fallback for missed/JIT syscalls. It
242	  requires per-thread setup and difficult signal/alt-stack/exec/clone handling.
243	- Frida and QBDI are active but require substantial custom syscall semantics.
244	- Intel Pin is proprietary. E9Patch is GPL and lacks complete dynamic/JIT
245	  lifecycle coverage. zpoline's page-zero/SELinux requirements rule it out as
246	  the production default. Pure eBPF cannot implement Reverie's replace,
247	  injection, memory, lifecycle, and signal contract.
248	
249	### KVM backend
250	
251	The KVM design's central result is that KVM provides an execution boundary,
252	not a Linux syscall implementation. gVisor runs application code at guest ring
253	3 and routes `SYSCALL` into Sentry code at guest ring 0; the Sentry implements
254	Linux process, memory, signal, futex, and syscall behavior.
255	
256	The proposed architecture is a versioned Sentry bridge plus a Rust
257	`reverie-kvm` frontend. The Rust side owns tools and exposes `Guest`; the Sentry
258	owns virtual Linux tasks and publishes syscall, signal, thread, exec, and exit
259	events. A standalone Rust KVM loop would amount to building another Linux ABI
260	and is not the smaller option.
261	
262	Current implementation evidence is deliberately modest: a 310-line protocol
263	skeleton negotiates version, architecture, capabilities, and message bounds;
264	it passes `cargo check`, five unit tests, formatting, and diff checks. The
265	actual Sentry bridge is unimplemented. Retain the existing estimate of 4-6
266	engineer-months for an x86-64 MVP and 9-15 engineer-months for parity and
267	hardening. Start only after workload and backend benchmarks justify that
268	investment.

270	## Schedule search and concurrency testing
271	
272	### What works
273	
274	The existing `hermit analyze` event-level search is operational:
275	
276	- `hello_race` started 6,088,241 adjacent swaps apart, converged to one event
277	  pair in 22 passes, emitted both stacks, and localized
278	  `flaky-tests/hello_race.rs:37`.
279	- `racewrite_nostdlib` converged in six passes with zero desynchronizations,
280	  isolated adjacent write posthooks, and localized
281	  `tests/c/simple/racewrite_nostdlib.c:35`.
282	- Edit-distance tests pass 22/22, schedule-search unit tests pass 3/3, and the
283	  CLI builds and exposes `analyze`.
284	
285	The algorithm records normalized schedule-event blocks, constructs an
286	adjacent-swap path between opposite-outcome schedules, executes a midpoint,
287	and replaces one endpoint until the boundary is one swap apart. Precise PMU
288	RCB timers enforce branch blocks, and the final runs capture stacks. This is a
289	linear-path boundary search, not exhaustive schedule enumeration or direct
290	memory-race localization.
291	
292	### Known limitations
293	
294	- Replay jitter can label a requested midpoint with the outcome of a different
295	  realized schedule and can move outside the intended interval.
296	- `swap_distance == 1` does not prove that only one event differs; insertions
297	  and deletions may remain. Greedy exact-block matching is weak for loops and
298	  split RCB blocks.
299	- Partial branch-count consumption, blocked-thread rules, syscall-prehook
300	  switching, and robust resynchronization are incomplete.
301	- Advertised explicit endpoint schedule inputs are unimplemented.
302	- Branch-level `sub_event_search` has been disabled since the original public
303	  history. Its bounds, applicability, jitter, and final A/B validation are not
304	  safe enough to enable.
305	- No stability sampling separates a deterministic ordering violation from
306	  residual nondeterminism. Current events cannot localize inside branch-free
307	  instruction regions or identify the actual racing load/store.
308	
309	The research estimate is 4-6 weeks for a credible x86-64 PMU-backed MVP and
310	8-12 weeks for a supported feature. Exact memory-access localization is a
311	separate instrumentation project.
312	
313	### Chaos stress results
314	
315	Chaos already exposes logical ordering bugs across thread counts. Ten-seed
316	matrices found lost atomic updates, publish-ordering errors, missing barriers,
317	producer/consumer ordering bugs, and lost condvar wakeups at varying rates.
318	`hello_race` failed 5/20 seeds; `hello_race_mini` failed 11/20. An imprecise
319	timer profile found `cas_sequence_easy` 31/100 times and reproduced seed 2 in
320	5/5 attempts, while precise discovery was impractically slow.
321	
322	Two boundaries matter:
323	
324	- The current stress wrapper can falsely skip all PMU tests because it searches
325	  modern `perf list` output for the obsolete phrase `Hardware event` (issue
326	  #82). This must be fixed before treating the gate as evidence.
327	- Serialized guest threads do not simulate weak memory. A relaxed-atomic
328	  store-buffer outcome occurred natively but 0/40 times under Hermit chaos.
329	  Hermit is best at logical ordering, lifetime, locking, and filesystem
330	  invariants, not genuine simultaneous weak-memory behavior.
331	
332	## QEMU and Linux-kernel milestone
333	
334	### Measured QEMU surface
335	
336	The validated QEMU 10.1.0 TCG boot made 147,679 calls across 54 syscall names.
337	The dominant calls were futex (62,456), `ppoll` (33,589), write (22,390), read
338	(19,856), `writev` (2,889), `mprotect` (2,351), and `madvise` (2,003).
339	
340	Detcore has dedicated arms for 26 names representing 72.09% of calls, explicit
341	passthrough for 11 names representing 3.17%, and fallback behavior for 17 names
342	representing 24.73%. `ppoll` plus `writev` account for 99.87% of fallback call
343	volume. Dedicated dispatch is not the same as deterministic correctness:
344	
345	- `FUTEX_WAIT_BITSET|FUTEX_CLOCK_REALTIME` is treated as relative and has a
346	  nanosecond-conversion bug; QEMU used it 649 times.
347	- `ppoll` lacks scheduler and record/replay semantics.
348	- Vectored I/O lacks complete resource/nonblocking/replay behavior.
349	- `recvmsg` does not record control data or received FDs, which matters for the
350	  external vhost-user filesystem helper.
351	- `fcntl`, `mmap`, PID/TID/rseq, file metadata/offset calls, and JIT mapping
352	  behavior remain partial.
353	
354	KVM mode is not the first target. It made 54,981 ioctls, 83.6% of all calls;
355	deterministically modeling KVM fd state, `kvm_run` pages, guest memory effects,
356	interrupts, and VM/vCPU lifecycle is a months-scale architecture project.
357	
358	### Current execution result
359	
360	QEMU/TCG boots and exits successfully under Hermit when precise preemption,
361	thread sequentialization, time virtualization, metadata virtualization, and
362	CPUID virtualization are disabled. The same minimal boot can pass
363	`--panic-on-unsupported-syscalls`. This proves syscall interception reach, not
364	deterministic VM execution.
365	
366	Full deterministic mode remains non-viable today:
367	
368	- sequentialization causes extreme vCPU/I/O-thread slowdown;
369	- virtualized time causes guest TSC/APIC clock-skew warnings;
370	- precise preemption adds the measured CPU overhead;
371	- vng inherited-initrd fd handling and external helper/filesystem state need a
372	  reproducible launch model.
373	
374	### Kernel race-testing position
375	
376	Hermit should be presented as a schedule-control and replay layer, not as a
377	replacement for syzkaller or KCSAN and not as the first deterministic kernel
378	scheduler. Razzer, SKI, Snowboard, and KRACE already demonstrate directed or
379	systematic kernel concurrency testing.
380	
381	The defensible value is composability: hold a pinned QEMU/TCG image and guest
382	workload constant, make the host QEMU schedule a first-class replay artifact,
383	and compare passing/failing schedules with the existing order-search tooling.
384	Use guest KCSAN/KASAN/LOCKDEP/panic/invariants as the oracle and syzkaller or LTP
385	as workload generators. Start with known logical concurrency bugs and two TCG
386	vCPUs. Do not claim weak-memory, DMA, or real-parallel coverage.
387

415	## Dependencies and parallelism
416	
417	The critical dependency graph is:
418	
419	```text
420	truthful CI + exact coverage
421	  -> arbitrary-binary correctness
422	  -> stable run/record/replay
423	  -> schedule-search validity
424	  -> QEMU record/replay
425	  -> kernel race feasibility demo
426	
427	truthful CI + backend-neutral conformance
428	  -> SaBRe stabilization -----+
429	  -> DynamoRIO prototype -----+-> fast-backend selection
430	                                  -> useful backend
431	                                  -> process parallelism/parity
432	
433	PMU benchmark gate
434	  -> precise-preemption optimization
435	  -> practical schedule discovery and QEMU execution
436	
437	KVM/Sentry design + workload justification
438	  -> KVM bridge MVP
439	  -> parity/hardening
440	```
441	
442	Three workstreams can run in parallel after the P0 gate:
443	
444	1. Correctness and coverage: issues #76-#82, CI, port recovery, ordinary
445	   run/record/replay.
446	2. Performance and backends: precise PMU optimization, SaBRe stabilization,
447	   DynamoRIO proof of concept, common conformance benchmarks.
448	3. Schedule/QEMU: search validity work and strict TCG syscall/launch support.
449	
450	Integration checkpoints should occur at exact SHAs every one to two weeks.
451	Each checkpoint must publish test counts, benchmark commands, runner
452	capabilities, and known skips. Kernel experiments start only after the QEMU
453	verify checkpoint; KVM implementation starts only after a backend/workload
454	review explicitly funds the months-scale program.
455	
456	## Decision gates
457	
458	1. **CI gate:** no "green" claim while required namespace/PMU tests are skipped
459	   or the runner cannot execute full Hermit integration targets.
460	2. **Fast-backend gate:** choose a backend from conformance and workload data,
461	   not a single raw-syscall microbenchmark. Preserve the synchronous-subset
462	   option rather than forcing false shared-API parity.
463	3. **Schedule-search gate:** never attach an outcome to a requested schedule
464	   that did not execute. Report a critical pair only after a final passing and
465	   failing A/B replay validates that difference.
466	4. **QEMU gate:** establish strict TCG replay with immutable inputs before
467	   adding open-ended fuzzing, more devices, networking, or KVM.
468	5. **Kernel-race gate:** require a stable guest oracle and a known bug before
469	   measuring schedules/hour or attempting discovery claims.
470	6. **KVM gate:** do not treat the protocol skeleton as a backend. Fund the
471	   Sentry bridge only with a dedicated team and explicit ABI/security scope.
